content_html:
Return on investment, or ROI, measures how much you gained or lost compared with what you put in. It is the quickest way to judge whether an investment paid off. On its own, though, ROI ignores time: a 45% gain is impressive over three years and modest over twenty. This calculator shows the total ROI and the annualized ROI, the steady yearly rate that would produce the same result.

How to use this calculator

  1. Amount invested: what you paid to get into the investment.
  2. Amount returned: what you sold it for, or what it is worth now if you still hold it.
  3. Holding period: enter a length in years and months, or switch to start and end dates.
  4. More options: add income you received and kept, such as dividends or rent, and costs such as commissions or closing fees.

The ROI formulas

Total cost is the amount invested plus fees. Total received is the amount returned plus income. Then:

ROI = (total received − total cost) ÷ total cost

Annualized ROI = (total received ÷ total cost)1 ÷ years − 1

The annualized figure is a compound annual growth rate. It answers the question: what constant yearly return would turn the cost into the amount received over the same holding period? When you use dates, the holding period is the number of days between them divided by 365.25.

Worked example

You invest $10,000 and sell three years later for $14,500. The net gain is $4,500, so the ROI is $4,500 ÷ $10,000 = 45%. The annualized ROI is 1.451/3 − 1 = 13.19% a year. The table under the calculator shows the path: $11,318.51 after year one, then about $12,811 and finally $14,500.

Compare a second investment that turns $10,000 into $12,000 in one year. Its total ROI is only 20%, well below 45%, but its annualized ROI is also 20%, higher than 13.19%. Annualizing is what makes that comparison fair.

Getting a realistic ROI

  • Include every cost: trading commissions, closing costs, repairs on a property or advisory fees all reduce the true return.
  • Include income only if you kept it. Reinvested dividends are already part of the amount returned.
  • Annualized figures for holdings shorter than a year assume the same pace would continue, which can greatly overstate a lucky short-term gain.
  • Simple ROI works for one purchase and one sale. If you added or withdrew money along the way, an internal rate of return gives a more accurate yearly figure.

faq.question: What is a good ROI?
faq.answer: It depends on the risk and the time involved. A useful check is to compare the annualized ROI with what a low-risk alternative, such as a savings account or Treasury bill, paid over the same period. A higher-risk investment should be judged against that benchmark.

faq.question: Does ROI account for inflation?
faq.answer: No. ROI is a nominal figure. To see the real return, subtract the inflation rate over the same period from the annualized ROI as a rough guide, or adjust the amounts with an inflation calculator.

faq.question: Can ROI be negative?
faq.answer: Yes. If you receive less than your total cost, the ROI is negative and the calculator shows a net loss. A total loss gives an ROI of −100%.

faq.question: Should taxes be included in ROI?
faq.answer: You can include them as a cost if you want an after-tax figure. Many people compare pre-tax ROI across investments first, then check the tax treatment separately, because tax depends on the account and your situation.

faq.question: What is the difference between ROI and IRR?
faq.answer: ROI looks only at the start and end amounts. IRR accounts for the timing of every cash flow, so it handles investments with several contributions or withdrawals. For a single purchase and a single sale with no income in between, annualized ROI and IRR give the same yearly rate.
